submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on a token whose last character is the vowel letter o - Latin o/O, Greek omicron and omega (ο/ό/ω), Cyrillic о/О, katakana syllables with the vowel o (オ/コ/ソ/ト/ロ/...), Arabic و - when that token is a piece of a word the model is spelling out across several tokens rather than a whole familiar word: mid-word o-final fragments of rare, technical or foreign vocabulary (Alopiidae, allozyme, cyclophosphamide, Ploče, Françoise), URL strings, and Greek text written character-by-character. It stays near zero for any o inside a common whole-word token (to, of, on, no, so, two, who, also, into, do, too, video), for a rare word that is merely mentioned rather than expected ('The word Alopiidae'), and for an o that closes a word (word-final Greek ο); its output suppresses o-initial word-continuation tokens, i.e. it cancels the o it has just read.

So what is this word "pooshnowb?" You may have heard Sara and Cliff use this word when talking to one another. Well, the truth is, it really depends on who you ask! Pooshnowb can have various meanings, as you can see below -- but it's definitions are virtually unlimited.
Pooshnowb (POO-sh'NOWB) -adj., n., v.
1. The act of being difficult; argumentative (alt., adj.) "Why you gotta be such a pooshnowb?"
2. Random body parts: "Did you forget to wash your pooshnowb?"
3. A delightful treat: "Don't eat your pooshnowb!!! You'll ruin your supper!!"
4. Term of endearment; pet name for spouse or significant other: "I love my li'l Pooshnowb. Yyyyye-us."
We definitely can't take credit for this word. Words like pooshnowb were first used by Chad Muncy, brother of Cliff Muncy. At a young age, Chad expressed an interest in creating his own language. Over time this language has evolved to include a myriad of words -- "pooshnowb" being one of them. Cliff and others have taken his lead and are always looking to create new words with new meanings. As a side note, Chad now has a son to whom he is teaching this new language. We look forward to seeing how the other kindergarteners will react to this behavior.
Pooshnowb has several word cousins including "shnoobowb" and "shnowboob". These words can be used interchangeably and even all in the same sentence. For instance, "You need to wash your pooshnowb, you little shnowboob!"
It has been recently discovered that by adding various endings onto pooshnowb and its word cousins, one can obtain even a larger number of definitions. For example, "Would you please wash your shnoobowb, you little shnoobowbulite! You're going to catch shnoobowbulitus!"

‘El Perro’ is one of Goya’s Black Paintings that was part of the decoration in his country house, the Quinta del Sordo. The painting depicts a dog staring at a featureless wall, representing the gloom and futility that Goya felt in his old age. Despite being deaf, Goya is shown painting in the silence and solitude of his home. "St. Jerome in his study" is a painting of St. Jerome, who was a Christian scholar and theologian, in his study. He is shown sitting at a table with a skull at his feet and a crucifix on the wall behind him. The painting is known for its somber tone, with muted colors and a sense of loneliness and despair.

"Melancolia 1" is a print that shows a female figure sitting in deep thought with a variety of objects scattered around her, including a compass, a book, and other tools. The figure is often interpreted as a personification of melancholy, with the objects representing different aspects of human knowledge and creativity. The print is known for its intricate detail and use of symbolism.

Both of these works, as well as the other Black Paintings, were created late in Goya's life, during a period of personal and political turmoil. adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The deep sea remains one of the least explored environments on Earth. Below roughly one thousand metres, sunlight fades completely, and the animals that live there have evolved remarkable adaptations to darkness, cold and crushing pressure. Research vessels working in the Pacific have documented glowing fish, glass sponges and dense communities clustered around volcanic vents. For decades, biologists assumed that such ecosystems depended almost entirely on organic matter sinking from the surface. That assumption changed in 1977, when submersible pilots observed tubeworms and clams crowded around warm mineral chimneys on a rift in the eastern Pacific. Chemosynthetic bacteria, the pilots realised, were converting hydrogen sulphide into energy and forming the base of a food web that owed nothing to the sun.

Since then, expeditions have mapped vent fields along the East Pacific Rise, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the back-arc basins of the western Pacific. Each site hosts species found nowhere else, and the catalogue of new genera grows every year. Camera sleds and gliders now survey these landscapes in detail, capturing footage of snailfish at eight thousand metres and of bacterial mats coating basalt surfaces. Sediment cores lifted from abyssal plains contain tiny shells that record millions of years of ocean chemistry, allowing scientists to reconstruct temperature, circulation and surface productivity across deep time.

The engineering challenges are considerable. Pressure at the bottom of the Mariana Trench is immense, and instruments must survive corrosive seawater and near-freezing temperatures. Titanium housings, oil-filled compensators and fibre-optic tethers have gradually extended the reach of human observation. A modern remotely operated vehicle can descend for twelve hours, collect samples with manipulator arms and stream high-definition video to a control room thousands of kilometres away. Recordings from these dives are archived and shared openly, so that a student in Lisbon can analyse footage gathered above the Kermadec Trench.

Advances in genomics have transformed the field as well. DNA extracted from a single amphipod can now be sequenced within a day, revealing which genes are switched on at abyssal pressures. Comparative studies suggest that several lineages independently evolved similar solutions, from stabilising proteins to accumulating osmolytes that protect membranes from collapse. Genetic tools have also made it possible to identify larvae drifting in the water column, linking adults on one seamount to juveniles on another hundreds of kilometres away. Such findings hint at corridors of connectivity that conservation planners are only beginning to map.

Explaining how animals sense their surroundings at such depths requires patient physiological work. In the laboratory, researchers keep specimens in darkened tanks and measure the neurophysiology of pressure tolerance.
